senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Curiosity – and, alone and sharp, a slightly rude “What?”.

senses.def: something (= etwas, colloquial: Ich habe was gefunden)

examples.tr: What are you drinking?
What is this?

examples.text: Alles, was du brauchst, ist im Kühlschrank.
examples.tr: Everything you need is in the fridge.
Do you want something to eat?

synonyms.nuance: “Pardon?” – the polite way to ask someone to repeat; a bare Was? sounds rude

etymology.text: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, English what, Danish hvad.

funFacts: German w- question words match English wh- words: was – what, wo – where, wer – who (careful!).
pitfalls: False friend: German was = what, not the English past tense “was” (that is war).
After prepositions standard German uses wo(r)- + preposition: Womit? Worüber? – mit was is colloquial.
subtleties: Was? alone sounds abrupt; Wie bitte? is the polite version.

profile.feeling: Searching for something – the keys, the station, the garlic.

senses.def: where (relative: die Stadt, wo ich wohne)

examples.tr: Where is the potato?
Excuse me, where is the station?

examples.text: Das ist die Stadt, wo ich geboren bin.
examples.tr: That's the town where I was born.

examples.text: Ich habe meine Brille wo liegen lassen.
examples.tr: I've left my glasses somewhere.

synonyms.nuance: at which place – stiff, written

etymology.text: With a widespread dialectal shift from -ā- to -ō-, from Middle High German wā, wār, from Old High German wār, hwār, from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwēr, *hwar; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, whence also wer. Cognate with English where.

funFacts: The old -r of wo (compare English where) survives in compounds: woran, worauf, worin.
pitfalls: wo is only for location: wohin = where to (Wohin gehst du?), woher = where from (Woher kommst du?).
False friend: German wo = where, German wer = who.
subtleties: In southern German speech wo is also used as a relative pronoun (der Mann, wo …) – nonstandard.

senseForms.note: the genitive (formal); in speech: von wem?

profile.feeling: A face at the door, a voice on the phone: Wer ist da? – the question about a person.

senses.def: whose? – the genitive wessen (formal); in speech: von wem? / wem gehört …?

examples.tr: Who is that?
Who do you live with?
Who are you looking for?
Whose bag is this?

examples.text: Von wem ist das Buch? – Von meiner Schwester.
examples.tr: Whose book is it? – My sister’s.
Is anybody there?

examples.text: Wer zu spät kommt, muss draußen warten.
examples.tr: Whoever comes late has to wait outside.

phrases.text: Wer zuletzt lacht, lacht am besten.
phrases.meaning: he who laughs last laughs longest

phrases.text: Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen.
phrases.tr: Whoever says A must also say B.
phrases.meaning: once you start something, you have to go on with it

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: wer is the only word for “who?”; welcher asks “which one” from a known set.

etymology.text: From Middle High German wër, from Old High German wër, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ. Related to wo; compare English who.

funFacts: wer, wen, wem, wessen end like the article der, den, dem, des – learn the two sets together.
One Indo-European question root *kʷ- is behind German wer, was, wo, English who, what, where, Latin quis, Greek τίς and Russian кто, что.
pitfalls: wer = who, wo = where – a classic mix-up (English “where” looks like wer).
Choose the case: Wer kocht? (subject) – Wen fragst du? (object) – Mit wem? (dative) – Wessen? (owner).
wer takes a singular verb (Wer kocht heute?) – except when sein links it to a plural noun: Wer sind diese Leute?
subtleties: wessen sounds formal or written; everyday speech says Von wem ist das? or Wem gehört das?
wer has no feminine and no plural: it asks about a man, a woman or several people alike.

profile.feeling: Making plans and checking times – When do we eat? When does the train leave?

senses.def: when? (at what time; also in indirect questions: Ich weiß nicht, wann …)

examples.tr: When are we eating?

examples.text: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?
examples.tr: When does the train to Berlin leave?
How long have you been living here?

examples.text: Bis wann bist du im Büro?
examples.tr: Until when are you at the office?
Drop by sometime!

phrases.meaning: now and then, from time to time

synonyms.nuance: at what time – for clock times only
at what time – stiff, written

etymology.text: From Middle High German wanne, Old High German wanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannā, *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan. Cognate with English when.

funFacts: English “when” is three German words: wann (question), wenn (whenever, if) and als (once, in the past).
pitfalls: wann asks (also in indirect questions: Weißt du, wann …?). The “when” that joins two clauses is wenn or als (S18): Wenn ich Zeit habe, … – not *Wann ich Zeit habe.
subtleties: For a clock time Germans often ask Um wie viel Uhr …?; Wann …? is wider (a day, a time of day, a date).

profile.feeling: The everyday question word: names, the weather, how things are going.

senses.def: how (+ adjective or adverb): wie alt, wie groß, wie lange
as, like (comparison: so groß wie …, wie immer)

examples.tr: What’s your name? (literally: How are you called?)

examples.text: Wie ist das Wetter in Athen?
examples.tr: What’s the weather like in Athens?
How old are you?

examples.text: Er ist so groß wie sein Vater.
examples.tr: He is as tall as his father.

phrases.text: Wie man sich bettet, so liegt man.
phrases.tr: As one makes one’s bed, so one lies.
phrases.meaning: you have to live with the consequences of your choices

synonyms.nuance: in what way – asks only about the manner

etymology.text: From Middle High German wie, a merger of Old High German hwio (from Proto-Germanic *hwaiwa) and hwē, hwie (from Proto-Germanic *hwē), a fossilized instrumental of the question stem *hwaz, *hwat (“who, what”).

funFacts: Greek and Russian ask the name with “how” too: Πώς σε λένε; – Как тебя зовут? Turkish asks “what”: Adın ne?
pitfalls: “What’s your name?” is Wie heißt du? / Wie heißen Sie? – not *Was heißt du? (Was heißt …? asks what a word means: Was heißt „Haus“ auf Griechisch?).
wie viel = how much; “how many” before a plural is wie viele.
subtleties: Wie? alone is a casual “what?/pardon?”; Wie bitte? is the polite form.
so … wie = as … as (so alt wie ich); after a comparative German uses als: älter als ich.

profile.feeling: Curiosity, sometimes reproach: Why? Why not?

examples.tr: Why don’t you drink coffee?

examples.text: Warum ist der Laden heute zu?
examples.tr: Why is the shop closed today?
Are you coming along? – Why not?

examples.text: Ich weiß nicht, warum er nicht hier ist.
examples.tr: I don’t know why he isn’t here.

synonyms.nuance: why – very common in speech, a little softer
why – a little more formal or written
what for – asks about the purpose, not the cause

etymology.text: From Middle High German warumme, war umbe, from Old High German wār umbe; equivalent to wo (“where”) + um (“for the purpose of”), thus “for what purpose”. Doublet of worum. Compare Dutch waarom.

funFacts: warum is built like Greek γιατί (για + τι, “for what”), Russian почему (по + чему) and Turkish neden (ne + den, “from what”): every language asks “for/from what?”.
pitfalls: The answer usually starts with weil, and the verb goes to the end (S18): Warum? – Weil ich müde bin.
subtleties: Warum nicht? is also a relaxed “yes”: Kaffee? – Warum nicht?

contrasts.value: with a mass noun (wie viel Zucker); colloquially also with a plural

profile.feeling: Shopping and cooking: how much sugar, how much money?

senses.def: how much? (before an uncountable noun, or alone)
how many? (colloquial, before a plural noun – standard: wie viele)

examples.tr: How much sugar would you like?
How much does this cost?
What time is it?

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; for clock times Germans also ask Wann? or Um wie viel Uhr?

etymology.text: Univerbation of wie + viel; the one-word spelling wieviel was standard until the 1996 spelling reform.

funFacts: Greek πόσο / πόσοι, Russian сколько and Turkish kaç / ne kadar split “how much” and “how many” in their own ways – German does it with one ending: viel / viele.
pitfalls: wie viel + singular (uncountable) – wie viel Wasser; with a plural noun use wie viele: wie viele Äpfel.
Two words today (wie viel); the older spelling wieviel is still often seen.
subtleties: In everyday speech wie viel also comes before plurals (Wie viel Kinder hast du?), but written standard German says wie viele.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Counting people and things: how many children, how many rooms?

senses.def: how many? (before a plural noun; declines like viele: mit wie vielen …)

examples.tr: How many children do you have?
How many people are here?

examples.text: Mit wie vielen Leuten wohnst du zusammen?
examples.tr: How many people do you live with?

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in standard German; colloquially many people say wie viel before plurals too.

etymology.text: From wie (“how”) + viele, the plural of viel (“much”).

funFacts: The question word and its noun stay together in first place: Wie viele Brüder hast du? – never *Wie viele hast du Brüder? in standard German.
pitfalls: wie viele goes with plural nouns (wie viele Äpfel); for uncountable things use wie viel (wie viel Milch).
After a dative preposition it takes -n: mit wie vielen Kindern.
subtleties: The answer is a number or viele / wenige / keine: Wie viele? – Drei.

contrasts.value: some, any – standing for a noun already named (Ich habe welche)

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: A choice in front of you: which bag, which tea, which bus?

senses.def: which? what? (choosing from a known set; declines like dieser)
some, any (as a pronoun: Hast du Milch? – Ja, ich habe welche.)

examples.tr: Which bus goes to the station?
Which bag is yours?
Which tea would you like?

examples.text: Hast du Milch? – Ja, im Kühlschrank ist welche.
examples.tr: Do you have milk? – Yes, there’s some in the fridge.

examples.text: Der Mann, welcher dort steht, ist mein Vater.
examples.tr: The man who is standing there is my father.

examples.text: Ich habe keine Äpfel mehr. Hast du welche?
examples.tr: I have no apples left. Do you have any?

synonyms.nuance: what kind of – asks for the kind, not for one item of a known set

etymology.text: From Middle High German welich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz. Compare English which.

funFacts: welcher and English which go back to one Germanic word *hwi-līk- “what-like”; the same *-līk- is in English such and German solcher.
pitfalls: welcher declines like dieser (and der): welcher Mann, welche Frau, welches Kind; accusative welchen Mann; dative welchem Mann.
English “what + noun” is often welcher in German: What colour? – Welche Farbe?
subtleties: Welcher …? picks from things you can see or know; Was für ein …? asks about the type: Was für ein Auto hast du? – Ein kleines.
Colloquial welche = “some”: Ich habe welche. (I have some.)

lexemes.role: by profession – the phrase of the job question: Was sind Sie von Beruf? (What do you do for a living?)

profile.feeling: Small talk with someone new: name, where from – and the job.

senses.def: by profession, by trade (Was sind Sie von Beruf? – Ich bin Ärztin.)

examples.tr: What do you do for a living?
What do you do (for a living)?

examples.text: Er ist von Beruf Koch, aber er malt gern.
examples.tr: He is a cook by profession, but he likes painting.

collocations.tr: to be a teacher by profession

synonyms.nuance: as an adverb: Was machst du beruflich? – the most common everyday question
What work do you do? – direct, common in speech

etymology.text: From von (“of, from”) + Beruf (“occupation, profession”), from berufen (“to call”), literally “calling”.

funFacts: Beruf, like English “vocation” (Latin vocare, “to call”), means “a calling”; Max Weber traced its double sense – trade and calling from God – to Luther’s Bible translation.
pitfalls: The answer has no article: Ich bin Ärztin. – not *Ich bin eine Ärztin.
The question is Was …?, not *Wer bist du von Beruf? (wer asks who you are, not your job).
subtleties: Beruf is a trained profession (a calling); a job is die Stelle or, informally, der Job.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: White coat, waiting room, a prescription – the family doctor (Hausarzt) is the first stop.

senses.def: doctor, physician (male or of unspecified gender)

examples.tr: I am a doctor.
I have to go to the doctor tomorrow.

examples.text: Der Arzt sagt, ich soll im Bett bleiben.
examples.tr: The doctor says I should stay in bed.

examples.text: In der Stadt gibt es viele Ärzte.
examples.tr: There are many doctors in the town.

phrases.text: Fragen Sie Ihren Arzt oder Apotheker.
phrases.meaning: the closing line of every German medicine advert (… zu Risiken und Nebenwirkungen …)

synonyms.nuance: the doctor in everyday speech – also the academic title Dr.
a medical professional; someone who studied medicine

etymology.text: From Middle High German arzet, arzāt, from Old High German arzāt, from Latin archīāter (“physician”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχίατρος (arkhíatros, “chief physician”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἰατρός (iatrós, “healer”).

funFacts: Arzt comes from Greek ἀρχίατρος “chief physician” – the same ἰατρός as Greek γιατρός.
pitfalls: No article for a job after sein or werden: Ich bin Arzt – unless an adjective comes in: ein guter Arzt.
Plural with umlaut: die Ärzte; dative plural den Ärzten.
subtleties: Patients sometimes say Herr Doktor / Frau Doktor; the job itself is Arzt / Ärztin.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman doctor – most medical students in Germany today are women.

examples.tr: My sister is a doctor.

examples.text: Die Ärztin hat heute keine Zeit.
examples.tr: The doctor has no time today.

examples.text: Ist hier eine Ärztin oder ein Arzt?
examples.tr: Is there a doctor here?

synonyms.nuance: a woman who studied medicine; a medical professional

etymology.text: From Middle High German arzātīn, arzātinne. Equivalent to Arzt + -in, with umlaut.

funFacts: Several job feminines take an umlaut: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin, Anwalt → Anwältin, Bauer → Bäuerin.
pitfalls: Umlaut in the feminine: Arzt → Ärztin (not *Arztin).
No article for a job after sein: Sie ist Ärztin – unless an adjective comes in: eine gute Ärztin.
subtleties: Ärztinnen und Ärzte: official texts name both forms; the masculine plural Ärzte traditionally covers everyone.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Night shifts on a hospital ward – caring, hard work.

examples.tr: My brother is a nurse.
The nurse brings the food.
Nurses often work at night.

collocations.tr: geriatric nurse, carer for the elderly

synonyms.nuance: short form – also a keeper: Tierpfleger (zookeeper)
the official job title in Germany since 2020
nurse, care worker – gender-neutral, used in official texts

etymology.text: From Kranke(r) (“sick person”) + Pfleger (“carer”, from pflegen “to care for”).

funFacts: Kranken- means “of the sick”: das Krankenhaus is the “house of the sick”, the Krankenpfleger the “carer of the sick”.
pitfalls: The male counterpart of Krankenschwester is Krankenpfleger – there is no *Krankenbruder.
Plural = singular: die Krankenpfleger; dative plural den Krankenpflegern.
subtleties: Since 2020 the training in Germany is called Pflegefachfrau / Pflegefachmann; Krankenpfleger(in) remains the everyday word.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Caring and competent – the neutral, modern word for a woman nurse.

examples.tr: She is a nurse at the hospital.
The nurse takes the temperature.

examples.text: Krankenpflegerinnen und Krankenpfleger sind sehr wichtig.
examples.tr: Nurses are very important.

synonyms.nuance: the traditional everyday word – still very common, no longer an official title
the official job title in Germany since 2020

etymology.text: From Krankenpfleger + -in.

funFacts: Like Greek νοσηλεύτρια (from νόσος, “illness”), the German word names the illness: krank (sick) + Pflegerin (carer).
pitfalls: A long but regular word: feminine -in, plural -innen (die Krankenpflegerinnen).
subtleties: Many people still say Krankenschwester; Krankenpflegerin sounds neutral and professional.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: The traditional word for a nurse – still heard everywhere, though no longer an official title.

examples.tr: My mother was a nurse.
The nurse brings the pills.

examples.text: Sie arbeitet als Krankenschwester in einer Klinik.
examples.tr: She works as a nurse in a clinic.

synonyms.nuance: the neutral, more modern word
the official job title since 2020
as a form of address in hospitals: Schwester, können Sie mir helfen?

etymology.text: From Kranker (“sick person”) + Schwester (“sister”).

funFacts: The “sister” goes back to the nursing nuns and deaconesses. Hebrew אָחוֹת (aḥot) means both “sister” and “nurse”, and in British hospitals a senior nurse is still called “Sister”.
pitfalls: There is no masculine *Krankenbruder: a man is Krankenpfleger.
Plural -n: die Krankenschwestern.
subtleties: Official titles no longer use it (Gesundheits- und Krankenpflegerin from 2004, Pflegefachfrau since 2020), but it is still very common in everyday speech.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Bridges, machines, cars – the profession behind “Made in Germany”.

examples.tr: My father is an engineer.
The company is looking for two engineers.

examples.text: Er ist Ingenieur bei einer Autofirma.
examples.tr: He is an engineer at a car company.

synonyms.nuance: technician – a lower qualification, not a university-trained engineer

etymology.text: Borrowed from French ingénieur, ultimately from Latin ingenium (“talent, cleverness”).

funFacts: Russian инженер and German Ingenieur are the same French word; Greek says μηχανικός, and Turkish mühendis is the Arabic مُهَنْدِس (muhandis).
pitfalls: French spelling and sound: g like the s in “measure” [ʒ], -ieur [iøːɐ̯].
Plural Ingenieure (not *Ingenieurs); dative plural den Ingenieuren.
subtleties: In Germany and Austria the engineering degree is shown like a title on doorbells and letters: Dipl.-Ing. Müller.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman in a technical profession – still a minority, but growing.

examples.tr: I am an engineer.
The engineer explains the plan.
More and more women become engineers.

synonyms.nuance: technician – a lower qualification

etymology.text: From Ingenieur (“engineer”) + -in.

funFacts: German feminine job words with -in are as old as Middle High German (arzātīn, “woman doctor”).
pitfalls: The same French sound as Ingenieur; plural Ingenieurinnen.
subtleties: A woman says Ich bin Ingenieurin – German marks the sex of the person in the job word.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Behind the wheel of a bus, a taxi or a lorry.

examples.text: Er ist Fahrer bei einer Firma.
examples.tr: He is a driver for a company.

examples.text: Der Fahrer wartet vor dem Haus.
examples.tr: The driver is waiting in front of the house.
The bus driver is very friendly.

synonyms.nuance: a private driver; in Switzerland the normal word for a professional driver
driver of a vehicle (Austrian and Swiss official language)

etymology.text: From fahren (“to drive, to travel”) + -er.

funFacts: fahren is related to English fare, as in farewell (“go well”).
pitfalls: Plural = singular: die Fahrer; dative plural den Fahrern.
The person driven is a Fahrgast (passenger), not a Fahrer.
subtleties: fahren covers going by any vehicle, so Fahrer is anyone at the controls – also of a bike: der Radfahrer (cyclist).

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

override.meaning: Wiktionary defines Fahrerin only as the “female equivalent of Fahrer” (driver).

profile.feeling: A woman driving a bus, a taxi or a lorry.

examples.tr: My aunt is a driver.

examples.text: Die Busfahrerin hält an der Schule.
examples.tr: The bus driver stops at the school.

examples.text: Die Fahrerin bringt die Kinder zur Schule.
examples.tr: The driver takes the children to school.

synonyms.nuance: a private driver (female)

etymology.text: From Fahrer (“driver”) + -in.

funFacts: In German road signs and laws the neutral form is Fahrzeugführer (vehicle operator) – few people say it aloud.
pitfalls: Plural Fahrerinnen; no umlaut.
subtleties: A Beifahrerin is the woman in the passenger seat, not a second driver.

profile.feeling: A hot kitchen, a white hat, the smell of soup.

senses.def: cook, chef (male or of unspecified gender)

examples.text: Er ist Koch in einem Restaurant.
examples.tr: He is a cook in a restaurant.
The cook is cooking fish today.

examples.text: In der Küche arbeiten drei Köche.
examples.tr: Three cooks work in the kitchen.

phrases.meaning: too many cooks spoil the broth

synonyms.nuance: head chef – the boss of a restaurant kitchen
ship’s cook (sailors’ word)

etymology.text: From Middle High German koch, from Old High German choch, from Proto-West Germanic *kok, borrowed from Latin coquus (“cook”). Compare English cook.

funFacts: Koch is also a common surname – Robert Koch discovered the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882.
pitfalls: der Koch (the cook) – kochen (to cook) – die Küche (the kitchen): Der Koch kocht in der Küche.
Plural with umlaut: die Köche.
subtleties: German Chef means boss, not chef: the chef of a restaurant is der Küchenchef or Chefkoch.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman who cooks for a living – or a grandmother everyone praises.

examples.text: Sie ist Köchin in einem Hotel.
examples.tr: She is a cook in a hotel.

examples.text: Meine Oma ist eine gute Köchin.
examples.tr: My grandma is a good cook.
The cook tastes the soup.

synonyms.nuance: head chef (female)

etymology.text: From Koch + -in, with umlaut.

funFacts: Like Ärztin and Anwältin, Köchin shows how the feminine -in often brings an umlaut.
pitfalls: Umlaut: Koch → Köchin; plural Köchinnen.
With an adjective the article comes back: Sie ist Köchin – Sie ist eine gute Köchin.
subtleties: eine gute Köchin can describe any woman who cooks well, not only a professional.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: The person behind the counter who helps you find things.

senses.def: shop assistant, salesperson (male or of unspecified gender)

examples.tr: The shop assistant is very friendly.

examples.text: Er arbeitet als Verkäufer im Supermarkt.
examples.tr: He works as a shop assistant in the supermarket.

examples.text: Der Verkäufer und der Käufer sind sich einig.
examples.tr: The seller and the buyer agree.

synonyms.nuance: the official title of a trained retail salesperson
trader, dealer – usually owns or runs the business

etymology.text: From verkaufen (“to sell”) + -er. Cognate with Dutch verkoper.

funFacts: kaufen comes from Latin caupo (“small trader, innkeeper”) – a cousin of English cheap (Old English cēap, “trade”).
pitfalls: verkaufen = to sell, kaufen = to buy: the Verkäufer sells, the Käufer or Kunde buys.
Plural = singular: die Verkäufer; dative den Verkäufern.
subtleties: In a shop der Verkäufer is the assistant; in a contract it is the seller (Verkäufer – Käufer).

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses Verkäuferin as “(feminine) seller, vendor” – in a shop, the shop assistant / saleswoman.

profile.feeling: A woman serving customers in a shop, a bakery or a market stall.

examples.tr: The shop assistant is helping me.

examples.text: Meine Cousine ist Verkäuferin in einer Bäckerei.
examples.tr: My cousin is a shop assistant in a bakery.
Why don’t you ask the shop assistant?

collocations.tr: to work as a shop assistant

synonyms.nuance: the official title of a trained retail saleswoman

etymology.text: From Verkäufer + -in.

funFacts: The agent noun takes an umlaut: kaufen → Käufer, verkaufen → Verkäufer(in) – as in backen → Bäcker.
pitfalls: Umlaut stays: Verkäuferin (from verkaufen → Verkäufer).
Plural Verkäuferinnen.
subtleties: In German shops you call a shop assistant with Entschuldigung! – not with a title.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Overalls and helmets: a factory, a building site.

senses.def: worker, labourer (male or of unspecified gender) – usually manual work

examples.text: Er ist Arbeiter in einer Fabrik.
examples.tr: He is a worker in a factory.

examples.text: Die Arbeiter essen um zwölf Uhr.
examples.tr: The workers eat at twelve o’clock.

examples.text: In den 1960er-Jahren kamen viele Arbeiter aus Griechenland und der Türkei.
examples.tr: In the 1960s many workers came from Greece and Turkey.

synonyms.nuance: employee – the legal term for anyone employed
salaried (office) employee – traditionally the opposite of the manual Arbeiter

etymology.text: From Middle High German arbeiter; by surface analysis arbeiten (“to work”) + -er.

funFacts: From 1960 (Greece) and 1961 (Turkey) West Germany recruited Gastarbeiter; many Greek and Turkish families in Germany go back to them.
pitfalls: Arbeiter usually means a manual worker; an office worker is ein Angestellter.
Plural = singular: die Arbeiter; dative den Arbeitern.
subtleties: die Arbeit (work) – arbeiten (to work) – der Arbeiter (worker): one family of words.

profile.feeling: A woman in a factory – or a busy worker bee.

examples.text: Sie ist Arbeiterin in einer Fabrik.
examples.tr: She is a worker in a factory.
The (women) workers get more money.

examples.text: Die Arbeiterin bringt Nektar in den Bienenstock.
examples.tr: The worker bee brings nectar into the hive.

synonyms.nuance: employee (female) – legal term

etymology.text: From Arbeiter (“labourer, worker”) + -in.

funFacts: Arbeit is related to Russian работа (rabota) – and to “robot”, from Czech robota (forced labour).
pitfalls: Plural Arbeiterinnen; no umlaut.
subtleties: In beekeeping die Arbeiterin is the worker bee – all worker bees are female.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Fields, cows and a farmhouse – and in chess, the humble pawn.

examples.tr: The farmer has many cows.
My grandpa was a farmer.

examples.text: Der Bauer kann nur nach vorne ziehen.
examples.tr: The pawn can only move forward.

examples.text: Du Bauer, kannst du nicht mal danke sagen?
examples.tr: You boor, can’t you even say thank you?

phrases.text: Was der Bauer nicht kennt, frisst er nicht.
phrases.tr: What the farmer doesn’t know, he doesn’t eat.
phrases.meaning: people refuse what is new to them

synonyms.nuance: the professional, official word for a farmer
countryman, farmer – old-fashioned

etymology.text: From Middle High German būre, gebūre, from Old High German būr (“peasant”), gibūr, gibūro, from Proto-West Germanic *būr, from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“inhabitant, dweller”). Compare English boor.

funFacts: The same word gave Dutch boer (whence the Boers of South Africa) and is hidden in Nachbar, “the one who dwells near” – like English neighbour.
pitfalls: Bauer is a weak (n-)noun in standard German: den Bauern, dem Bauern, des Bauern – the same form as the plural.
It can sound condescending (= country bumpkin); Landwirt is the neutral professional word.
subtleties: In chess der Bauer is the pawn; in some card games the jack is called Bauer.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: The farmer’s wife of old pictures – today a farmer in her own right.

examples.text: Die Bäuerin verkauft Eier auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: The farmer sells eggs at the market.
My grandmother was a farmer.
The farmer milks the cows.

synonyms.nuance: the professional, official word

etymology.text: From Bauer (“peasant”) + -in.

funFacts: Bauer and Bäuerin are related to bauen, which once meant “to dwell” and “to till the land” – today “to build”.
pitfalls: Umlaut: Bauer → Bäuerin (also spelled Bäurin); plural Bäuerinnen.
subtleties: Traditionally die Bäuerin also meant the farmer’s wife; today it is the job of a woman farmer.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Tractors, subsidies and modern farming – the professional word.

senses.def: farmer, agriculturist (male or of unspecified gender)

examples.tr: My uncle is a farmer.

examples.text: Viele Landwirte verkaufen ihre Milch an eine Molkerei.
examples.tr: Many farmers sell their milk to a dairy.

examples.text: Der Landwirt arbeitet den ganzen Tag auf dem Feld.
examples.tr: The farmer works in the field all day.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word – can sound rustic
a large-scale farmer, especially overseas (America, Africa)

etymology.text: Land (“land”) + Wirt (“host; caretaker”); chiefly a back-formation from Landwirtschaft (“agriculture”).

funFacts: Landwirtschaft (agriculture) is literally “land-economy” – Wirtschaft alone means economy, and also a pub.
pitfalls: Wirt alone is a landlord or innkeeper (der Gastwirt): the Landwirt “runs the land”.
Plural Landwirte; dative den Landwirten.
subtleties: Politicians and newspapers say Landwirte; people in the village say Bauern.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman running a farm – the professional title.

examples.tr: My aunt is a farmer.
The farmer has twenty cows.
More and more women become farmers.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word

etymology.text: From Landwirt (“farmer”) + -in.

funFacts: Wirtin alone is a landlady or the woman who runs a pub.
pitfalls: Plural Landwirtinnen; no umlaut.
subtleties: Landwirtin is the title of the trained profession; Bäuerin is how neighbours talk.

profile.feeling: A uniform, a patrol car – help, or a fine.

senses.def: police officer (male or of unspecified gender), policeman

examples.tr: My neighbour is a police officer.

examples.text: Der Polizist fragt nach meinem Ausweis.
examples.tr: The police officer asks for my ID.
Why don’t you ask the police officer?

synonyms.nuance: police officer – official
cop – pejorative, can be insulting
constable, bobby

etymology.text: From Polizei (“police”) + -ist; Polizei from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”), from πόλις (pólis, “city”).

funFacts: Polizist goes back to Greek πόλις, like Politik and Greek πολίτης.
pitfalls: Weak noun: den Polizisten, dem Polizisten, des Polizisten (all with -en).
die Polizei (the police force) is singular: Die Polizei kommt.
subtleties: Bulle is common slang but rude to an officer’s face.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman in uniform – a policewoman.

examples.tr: My sister is a police officer.
The policewoman helps the child.

examples.text: Zwei Polizistinnen stehen vor der Bank.
examples.tr: Two policewomen are standing in front of the bank.

collocations.tr: to work as a police officer

synonyms.nuance: police officer (female) – official

etymology.text: From Polizist + -in.

funFacts: German police forces belong to the federal states (Länder); the Bundespolizei guards borders, airports and stations.
pitfalls: Unlike the weak Polizist, Polizistin has no case endings: die, der, der, die Polizistin.
subtleties: In German police ranks titles change (Polizeimeisterin, Kommissarin); in everyday speech: Polizistin.

profile.feeling: A suit, a briefcase, a court – someone who speaks for you.

senses.def: lawyer, attorney (male or of unspecified gender)

examples.tr: I need a lawyer.
He is a lawyer in Berlin.

examples.text: Die Anwälte sprechen mit dem Richter.
examples.tr: The lawyers are talking to the judge.

synonyms.nuance: the full official title
someone who studied law – not necessarily a practising lawyer
advocate – old-fashioned (still used in Switzerland)

etymology.text: From Middle High German anwalde, from Old High German anawalto (“one who has power over something”), from walten (“to rule, hold sway”).

funFacts: Anwalt shares the root of walten, Gewalt (power, force) and English wield.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Anwälte; dative den Anwälten.
A Staatsanwalt is the prosecutor – not a lawyer who defends you.
subtleties: Herr Rechtsanwalt / Frau Rechtsanwältin is how letters address a lawyer.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

override.meaning: Wiktionary defines Anwältin only as the “female equivalent of Anwalt” (lawyer).

profile.feeling: A woman lawyer – in court, in an office, on the phone with clients.

examples.tr: My mother is a lawyer.
The lawyer has many clients.

examples.text: Frau Rechtsanwältin, wir haben eine Frage.
examples.tr: Counsellor, we have a question.

synonyms.nuance: a woman who studied law

etymology.text: From Anwalt + -in.

funFacts: Women have been admitted as lawyers in Germany only since 1922.
pitfalls: Umlaut: Anwalt → Anwältin; plural Anwältinnen.
subtleties: In letters: Sehr geehrte Frau Rechtsanwältin …

profile.feeling: A studio, paint on the hands, an exhibition – or music on a stage.

examples.text: Er ist Künstler und malt Bilder.
examples.tr: He is an artist and paints pictures.

examples.text: Die Künstler zeigen ihre Bilder im Museum.
examples.tr: The artists show their pictures in the museum.

examples.text: Mein Onkel ist ein echter Lebenskünstler.
examples.tr: My uncle really knows how to enjoy life.

collocations.tr: someone who knows how to live well (with little)

synonyms.nuance: painter – also a house painter
a creative (designer, artist)

etymology.text: From Kunst (“art”) + -ler; Kunst is derived from können (“to be able”).

funFacts: Kunst comes from können – art as “what you can do”, like Greek τέχνη (skill, craft, art).
pitfalls: False friend: German Artist is a circus performer (acrobat); an artist is ein Künstler.
Plural = singular: die Künstler; dative den Künstlern.
subtleties: Lebenskünstler is half praise, half irony: someone who gets by happily with little.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: A woman painter, sculptor, musician or performer.

examples.tr: My friend is an artist.

examples.text: Die Künstlerin zeigt ihre Bilder in Wien.
examples.tr: The artist is showing her pictures in Vienna.
Many (women) artists live in Berlin.

synonyms.nuance: painter (female)

etymology.text: From Künstler (“artist”) + -in.

funFacts: Käthe Kollwitz was the first woman elected to the Prussian Academy of Arts (1919).
pitfalls: Plural Künstlerinnen.
subtleties: Artistin in German means a circus performer, not an artist.
